definition.text: Multinomial logistic regression is a statistical method that predicts the probabilities of more than two unordered outcomes from a set of explanatory variables.

facts.text: It is also called the multinomial logit, softmax regression or the maximum entropy classifier, among other names.
In discrete choice theory, each outcome's score is read as the utility a person gets from choosing it, with a random part standing for unmodelled factors.
Used for choices, it assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives: the odds between two options do not depend on what other options are present.
Many psychology studies show that people often violate this assumption.
In best–worst scaling studies it is often the first stage of analysis, giving average utilities for items.

definition.text: A probit model is a regression model for a dependent variable that can take only two values, built on the normal distribution.

facts.text: It estimates the probability that an observation with given characteristics falls into one of the two categories, the same problem logistic regression handles.
It can be motivated as a latent variable model, with the outcome showing whether an unobserved variable is positive.
It is usually estimated by maximum likelihood.
Chester Bliss coined the term in 1934, though the basic model goes back to Fechner in 1860.

definition.text: A random utility model describes a person's preferences when their choices are not fixed but depend on a random, unobserved state.

facts.text: Classic economics assumes a rational person picks the alternative with the highest utility, which can be inferred from observed choices.
In practice people facing the same alternatives may choose differently, so their choices look random to an observer.
The model gives each person a distribution over utility functions rather than a single one, and assumes rational behaviour given the hidden state.
Choice experiments assume how often item A is chosen over item B measures how much it is preferred.
A popular version was developed by Luce and Plackett.
